newsitem.title: UK: Metals trade calm despite Zaire turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Metals trade calm despite Zaire turmoil.

text.p: European metal traders showed remarkable calm despite the escalation of hostilities in Zaire which have this week moved into the mineral rich province of Shaba.
This area of the central African country produces cobalt, used extensively in super alloys and the aircraft industries, and was once a major world producer of copper, European traders said.

"Reports from Zaire that insurgents are advancing towards the Shaba cobalt-producing region have so far been greeted with indifference by the market," stockbrokers Macquarie said in a recent metals report.

Informed trade sources said that Zaire's state-owned mining company Gecamines was experiencing few problems following the fall of the strategic transport port of Kalemie on the shores of Lake Tanganyika.
The port of Kalemie is about 400 miles north of Lubumbashi, the hub of Shaba's cobalt and copper production and lays close to the border of Zambia.
On Monday the Zairean government said they had lost Kalemie and since then further advances deeper into Shaba had been made by the rebels.
"The port (Kalemie) has not been used to export either copper or cobalt for around a decade," one trader said.
"If anything Gecamines would only use Kalemie for local imports,.something they can do with out," he added.
Another close source to the producer said Gecamines is continuing to export its production through South Africa or Tanzania via Zambia, another copper and cobalt producer.
"I have been informed there is no panic in the mining belt and that production has been unaffected," the source said.
On Wednesday Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila gave President Mobutu Sese Seko until February 21 to surrender power or face a major rebel attack.
London traders continued to eye the developments in Zaire but were reluctant to chase high grade cobalt prices higher.
In fact after an initial knee jerk reaction high grade cobalt prices have slipped.
Traders opinions of price levels as always remained divided in this opaque market.
They ranged from around $23 per pound down to just below $19.
"Until the fighting hits the mining region there is unlikely to be any serious prices reaction," one trader said.
Zaire produces around 5,000 tonnes of cobalt annually, world supply is around 28,000 tonnes, of which 1,000 tonnes is of high grade quality.
A lack of investment in new and existing mining facilities and the belts' infrastructure has seen copper production dive dramatically.
London metal analysts estimate that production of contained metal has fallen from 500,000 tonnes in the early 1980s to 210,000 tonnes in 1987 and 33,000 tonnes in 1995.
Present production is hard to pindown, though several analyst believed that it was below 10,000 tonnes.
"Zairean copper production is a drop in the ocean and any supply problems are unlikely to have any serious impact on global copper prices," one trader said.
